## Detailed Description

template<typename T>  
class sf::Rect< T >

Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.

A rectangle is defined by its top-left corner and its size.

It is a very simple class defined for convenience, so its member variables (position and size) are public and can be accessed directly, just like the vector classes ([Vector2](classsf_1_1Vector2.html "Class template for manipulating 2-dimensional vectors.") and [Vector3](classsf_1_1Vector3.html "Utility template class for manipulating 3-dimensional vectors.")).

To keep things simple, [sf::Rect](classsf_1_1Rect.html "Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.") doesn't define functions to emulate the properties that are not directly members (such as right, bottom, etc.), it rather only provides intersection functions.

[sf::Rect](classsf_1_1Rect.html "Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.") uses the usual rules for its boundaries:

* The left and top edges are included in the rectangle's area
* The right and bottom edges are excluded from the rectangle's area

This means that [sf::IntRect](namespacesf.html#add1cf75a734c8414680b0424145c30b1)({0, 0}, {1, 1}) and [sf::IntRect](namespacesf.html#add1cf75a734c8414680b0424145c30b1)({1, 1}, {1, 1}) don't intersect.

[sf::Rect](classsf_1_1Rect.html "Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.") is a template and may be used with any numeric type, but for simplicity type aliases for the instantiations used by SFML are given:

* [sf::Rect](classsf_1_1Rect.html "Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.")<int> is [sf::IntRect](namespacesf.html#add1cf75a734c8414680b0424145c30b1)
* [sf::Rect](classsf_1_1Rect.html "Utility class for manipulating 2D axis aligned rectangles.")<float> is [sf::FloatRect](namespacesf.html#a701020eb396e62ba560619e68c689a38)

So that you don't have to care about the template syntax.

Usage example:

// Define a rectangle, located at (0, 0) with a size of 20x5

[sf::IntRect](namespacesf.html#add1cf75a734c8414680b0424145c30b1) r1({0, 0}, {20, 5});

// Define another rectangle, located at (4, 2) with a size of 18x10

[sf::Vector2i](namespacesf.html#af0ffe1b157a56931ee3a9a1a771a827a) [position](#a561ce610acfafc975647c19db1c76bce)(4, 2);

[sf::Vector2i](namespacesf.html#af0ffe1b157a56931ee3a9a1a771a827a) [size](#a39912541f559c5f780e4400831595acc)(18, 10);

[sf::IntRect](namespacesf.html#add1cf75a734c8414680b0424145c30b1) r2([position](#a561ce610acfafc975647c19db1c76bce), [size](#a39912541f559c5f780e4400831595acc));

// Test intersections with the point (3, 1)

bool b1 = r1.contains({3, 1}); // true

bool b2 = r2.contains({3, 1}); // false

// Test the intersection between r1 and r2

std::optional<sf::IntRect> result = r1.findIntersection(r2);

// result.has\_value() == true

// result.value() == sf::IntRect({4, 2}, {16, 3})

## Detailed Description

Specialized shape representing a rectangle.

This class inherits all the functions of [sf::Transformable](classsf_1_1Transformable.html "Decomposed transform defined by a position, a rotation and a scale.") (position, rotation, scale, bounds, ...) as well as the functions of [sf::Shape](classsf_1_1Shape.html "Base class for textured shapes with outline.") (outline, color, texture, ...).

Usage example:

[sf::RectangleShape](classsf_1_1RectangleShape.html) rectangle;

rectangle.[setSize](#a9a07ce94a8f8da13164e6fc316d36fb8)([sf::Vector2f](namespacesf.html#af14b40e82368dd601a7ef8037214804d)(100, 50));

rectangle.[setOutlineColor](classsf_1_1Shape.html#a7dbbed35b7544a9e592acd3908713256)([sf::Color::Red](classsf_1_1Color.html#a127dbf55db9c07d0fa8f4bfcbb97594a));

rectangle.[setOutlineThickness](classsf_1_1Shape.html#a5ad336ad74fc1f567fce3b7e44cf87dc)(5);

rectangle.[setPosition](classsf_1_1Transformable.html#a47c1375b57cbb0e513286e8d11f6dd4d)({10, 20});

...

window.draw(rectangle);

## [◆](#ac0e29425d908d5442060cc44790fe4da)getGlobalBounds()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [FloatRect](namespacesf.html#a701020eb396e62ba560619e68c689a38) sf::Shape::getGlobalBounds | ( |  | ) | const | | nodiscardinherited |

Get the global (non-minimal) bounding rectangle of the entity.

The returned rectangle is in global coordinates, which means that it takes into account the transformations (translation, rotation, scale, ...) that are applied to the entity. In other words, this function returns the bounds of the shape in the global 2D world's coordinate system.

This function does not necessarily return the *minimal* bounding rectangle. It merely ensures that the returned rectangle covers all the vertices (but possibly more). This allows for a fast approximation of the bounds as a first check; you may want to use more precise checks on top of that.

Returns
:   Global bounding rectangle of the entity

Set the fill color of the shape.

This color is modulated (multiplied) with the shape's texture if any. It can be used to colorize the shape, or change its global opacity. You can use [sf::Color::Transparent](classsf_1_1Color.html#a569b45471737f770656f50ae7bbac292 "Transparent (black) predefined color.") to make the inside of the shape transparent, and have the outline alone. By default, the shape's fill color is opaque white.

set the local origin of the object

The origin of an object defines the center point for all transformations (position, scale, rotation). The coordinates of this point must be relative to the top-left corner of the object, and ignore all transformations (position, scale, rotation). The default origin of a transformable object is (0, 0).

## [◆](#af8fb22bab1956325be5d62282711e3b6)setTexture()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Shape::setTexture | ( | const [Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html) \* | *texture*, | |  |  | bool | *resetRect* = false ) | | inherited |

Change the source texture of the shape.

The texture argument refers to a texture that must exist as long as the shape uses it. Indeed, the shape doesn't store its own copy of the texture, but rather keeps a pointer to the one that you passed to this function. If the source texture is destroyed and the shape tries to use it, the behavior is undefined. texture can be a null pointer to disable texturing. If resetRect is true, the TextureRect property of the shape is automatically adjusted to the size of the new texture. If it is false, the texture rect is left unchanged.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | texture | New texture |
    | resetRect | Should the texture rect be reset to the size of the new texture? |

See also
:   [getTexture](classsf_1_1Shape.html#af4c345931cd651ffb8f7a177446e28f7 "Get the source texture of the shape."), [setTextureRect](classsf_1_1Shape.html#a2029cc820d1740d14ac794b82525e157 "Set the sub-rectangle of the texture that the shape will display.")

## Detailed Description

Base class for all render targets (window, texture, ...)

[sf::RenderTarget](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html "Base class for all render targets (window, texture, ...)") defines the common behavior of all the 2D render targets usable in the graphics module.

It makes it possible to draw 2D entities like sprites, shapes, text without using any OpenGL command directly.

A [sf::RenderTarget](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html "Base class for all render targets (window, texture, ...)") is also able to use views ([sf::View](classsf_1_1View.html "2D camera that defines what region is shown on screen")), which are a kind of 2D cameras. With views you can globally scroll, rotate or zoom everything that is drawn, without having to transform every single entity. See the documentation of [sf::View](classsf_1_1View.html "2D camera that defines what region is shown on screen") for more details and sample pieces of code about this class.

On top of that, render targets are still able to render direct OpenGL stuff. It is even possible to mix together OpenGL calls and regular SFML drawing commands. When doing so, make sure that OpenGL states are not messed up by calling the pushGLStates/popGLStates functions.

While render targets are moveable, it is not valid to move them between threads. This will cause your program to crash. The problem boils down to OpenGL being limited with regard to how it works in multithreaded environments. Please ensure you only move render targets within the same thread.

See also
:   [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing."), [sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html "Target for off-screen 2D rendering into a texture."), [sf::View](classsf_1_1View.html "2D camera that defines what region is shown on screen")

## [◆](#a07a8da6e2a9e3ce5f36344e3d8e7c41a)mapCoordsToPixel() [2/2]

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [Vector2i](namespacesf.html#af0ffe1b157a56931ee3a9a1a771a827a) sf::RenderTarget::mapCoordsToPixel | ( | [Vector2f](namespacesf.html#af14b40e82368dd601a7ef8037214804d) | *point*, | |  |  | const [View](classsf_1_1View.html) & | *view* ) const | | nodiscard |

Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates.

This function finds the pixel of the render target that matches the given 2D point. In other words, it goes through the same process as the graphics card, to compute the final position of a rendered point.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (150, 75) in your 2D world may map to the pixel (10, 50) of your render target – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Point to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in target coordinates (pixels)

See also
:   [mapPixelToCoords](#a5ce02e4fd30e065c4dbeec239ae579b3 "Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates, using the current view.")

## [◆](#af7c5ec0787ffdcabfcee0f2b88dd4536)mapPixelToCoords() [2/2]

Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates.

This function finds the 2D position that matches the given pixel of the render target. In other words, it does the inverse of what the graphics card does, to find the initial position of a rendered pixel.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (10, 50) in your render target may map to the point (150, 75) in your 2D world – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

For render-windows, this function is typically used to find which point (or object) is located below the mouse cursor.

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Pixel to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in "world" units

See also
:   [mapCoordsToPixel](#ab473e0723ba16cf913deb03774c8458c "Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates, using the current view.")

## [◆](#a8d1998464ccc54e789aaf990242b47f7)pushGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| void sf::RenderTarget::pushGLStates | ( |  | ) |  |

Save the current OpenGL render states and matrices.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering. Combined with popGLStates, it ensures that:

* SFML's internal states are not messed up by your OpenGL code
* your OpenGL states are not modified by a call to a SFML function

More specifically, it must be used around code that calls draw functions. Example:

// OpenGL code here...

window.pushGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

window.popGLStates();

// OpenGL code here...

Note that this function is quite expensive: it saves all the possible OpenGL states and matrices, even the ones you don't care about. Therefore it should be used wisely. It is provided for convenience, but the best results will be achieved if you handle OpenGL states yourself (because you know which states have really changed, and need to be saved and restored). Take a look at the resetGLStates function if you do so.

See also
:   [popGLStates](#ad5a98401113df931ddcd54c080f7aa8e "Restore the previously saved OpenGL render states and matrices.")

## [◆](#aac7504990d27dada4bfe3c7866920765)resetGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| void sf::RenderTarget::resetGLStates | ( |  | ) |  |

Reset the internal OpenGL states so that the target is ready for drawing.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering, if you choose not to use pushGLStates/popGLStates. It makes sure that all OpenGL states needed by SFML are set, so that subsequent [draw()](#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39 "Draw a drawable object to the render target.") calls will work as expected.

Example:

// OpenGL code here...

glPushAttrib(...);

window.resetGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

glPopAttrib(...);

// OpenGL code here...

## [◆](#adc225ead22a70843ffa9b7eebefa0ce1)setActive()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | virtual bool sf::RenderTarget::setActive | ( | bool | *active* = true | ) |  | | nodiscardvirtual |

Activate or deactivate the render target for rendering.

This function makes the render target's context current for future OpenGL rendering operations (so you shouldn't care about it if you're not doing direct OpenGL stuff). A render target's context is active only on the current thread, if you want to make it active on another thread you have to deactivate it on the previous thread first if it was active. Only one context can be current in a thread, so if you want to draw OpenGL geometry to another render target don't forget to activate it again. Activating a render target will automatically deactivate the previously active context (if any).

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | active | true to activate, false to deactivate |

Returns
:   true if operation was successful, false otherwise

Reimplemented in [sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html#a30eda291b7b7179e7a0d1506c953a424), and [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html#a3f5476821139d5a7f0e4df19dab69b56).

## [◆](#a063db6dd0a14913504af30e50cb6d946)setView()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| void sf::RenderTarget::setView | ( | const [View](classsf_1_1View.html) & | *view* | ) |  |

Change the current active view.

The view is like a 2D camera, it controls which part of the 2D scene is visible, and how it is viewed in the render target. The new view will affect everything that is drawn, until another view is set. The render target keeps its own copy of the view object, so it is not necessary to keep the original one alive after calling this function. To restore the original view of the target, you can pass the result of [getDefaultView()](#a7741129e3ef7ab4f0a40024fca13480c "Get the default view of the render target.") to this function.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | view | New view to use |

See also
:   [getView](#adbf8dc5a1f4abbe15a3fbb915844c7ea "Get the view currently in use in the render target."), [getDefaultView](#a7741129e3ef7ab4f0a40024fca13480c "Get the default view of the render target.")

## Detailed Description

Target for off-screen 2D rendering into a texture.

[sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html "Target for off-screen 2D rendering into a texture.") is the little brother of [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.").

It implements the same 2D drawing and OpenGL-related functions (see their base class [sf::RenderTarget](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html "Base class for all render targets (window, texture, ...)") for more details), the difference is that the result is stored in an off-screen texture rather than being show in a window.

Rendering to a texture can be useful in a variety of situations:

* precomputing a complex static texture (like a level's background from multiple tiles)
* applying post-effects to the whole scene with shaders
* creating a sprite from a 3D object rendered with OpenGL
* etc.

Usage example:

// Create a new render-window

[sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html) window([sf::VideoMode](classsf_1_1VideoMode.html)({800, 600}), "SFML window");

// Create a new render-texture

[sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html) texture({500, 500});

// The main loop

while (window.[isOpen](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#aa43559822564ef958dc664a90c57cba0)())

{

// Event processing

// ...

// Clear the whole texture with red color

texture.clear([sf::Color::Red](classsf_1_1Color.html#a127dbf55db9c07d0fa8f4bfcbb97594a));

// Draw stuff to the texture

texture.draw(sprite); // sprite is a sf::Sprite

texture.draw(shape); // shape is a sf::Shape

texture.draw(text); // text is a sf::Text

// We're done drawing to the texture

texture.display();

// Now we start rendering to the window, clear it first

window.[clear](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#aee353fc2cd35edf0747e710301af3e4c)();

// Draw the texture

[sf::Sprite](classsf_1_1Sprite.html) sprite(texture.getTexture());

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(sprite);

// End the current frame and display its contents on screen

window.[display](classsf_1_1Window.html#adabf839cb103ac96cfc82f781638772a)();

}

Like [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing."), [sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html "Target for off-screen 2D rendering into a texture.") is still able to render direct OpenGL stuff. It is even possible to mix together OpenGL calls and regular SFML drawing commands. If you need a depth buffer for 3D rendering, don't forget to request it when calling RenderTexture::create.

|  |  | const [ContextSettings](structsf_1_1ContextSettings.html) & | *settings* = {} ) |

Construct a render-texture.

The last parameter, settings, is useful if you want to enable multi-sampling or use the render-texture for OpenGL rendering that requires a depth or stencil buffer. Otherwise it is unnecessary, and you should leave this parameter at its default value.

After creation, the contents of the render-texture are undefined. Call [RenderTexture::clear](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#aee353fc2cd35edf0747e710301af3e4c "Clear the entire target with a single color.") first to ensure a single color fill.

Parameters
:   |  |  |

| void sf::RenderTexture::display | ( |  | ) |  |

Update the contents of the target texture.

This function updates the target texture with what has been drawn so far. Like for windows, calling this function is mandatory at the end of rendering. Not calling it may leave the texture in an undefined state.

## [◆](#a8ca34c8b7e00793c1d3ef4f9a834f8cc)generateMipmap()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | bool sf::RenderTexture::generateMipmap | ( |  | ) |  | | nodiscard |

Generate a mipmap using the current texture data.

This function is similar to [Texture::generateMipmap](classsf_1_1Texture.html#a7779a75c0324b5faff77602f871710a9 "Generate a mipmap using the current texture data.") and operates on the texture used as the target for drawing. Be aware that any draw operation may modify the base level image data. For this reason, calling this function only makes sense after all drawing is completed and display has been called. Not calling display after subsequent drawing will lead to undefined behavior if a mipmap had been previously generated.

Returns
:   true if mipmap generation was successful, false if unsuccessful

Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates.

This function finds the pixel of the render target that matches the given 2D point. In other words, it goes through the same process as the graphics card, to compute the final position of a rendered point.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (150, 75) in your 2D world may map to the pixel (10, 50) of your render target – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Point to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in target coordinates (pixels)

See also
:   [mapPixelToCoords](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a5ce02e4fd30e065c4dbeec239ae579b3 "Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates, using the current view.")

## [◆](#af7c5ec0787ffdcabfcee0f2b88dd4536)mapPixelToCoords() [2/2]

Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates.

This function finds the 2D position that matches the given pixel of the render target. In other words, it does the inverse of what the graphics card does, to find the initial position of a rendered pixel.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (10, 50) in your render target may map to the point (150, 75) in your 2D world – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

For render-windows, this function is typically used to find which point (or object) is located below the mouse cursor.

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Pixel to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in "world" units

See also
:   [mapCoordsToPixel](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ab473e0723ba16cf913deb03774c8458c "Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates, using the current view.")

## [◆](#a8d1998464ccc54e789aaf990242b47f7)pushGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::RenderTarget::pushGLStates | ( |  | ) |  | | inherited |

Save the current OpenGL render states and matrices.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering. Combined with popGLStates, it ensures that:

* SFML's internal states are not messed up by your OpenGL code
* your OpenGL states are not modified by a call to a SFML function

More specifically, it must be used around code that calls draw functions. Example:

// OpenGL code here...

window.pushGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

window.popGLStates();

// OpenGL code here...

Note that this function is quite expensive: it saves all the possible OpenGL states and matrices, even the ones you don't care about. Therefore it should be used wisely. It is provided for convenience, but the best results will be achieved if you handle OpenGL states yourself (because you know which states have really changed, and need to be saved and restored). Take a look at the resetGLStates function if you do so.

See also
:   [popGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ad5a98401113df931ddcd54c080f7aa8e "Restore the previously saved OpenGL render states and matrices.")

## [◆](#aac7504990d27dada4bfe3c7866920765)resetGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::RenderTarget::resetGLStates | ( |  | ) |  | | inherited |

Reset the internal OpenGL states so that the target is ready for drawing.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering, if you choose not to use pushGLStates/popGLStates. It makes sure that all OpenGL states needed by SFML are set, so that subsequent [draw()](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39 "Draw a drawable object to the render target.") calls will work as expected.

Example:

// OpenGL code here...

glPushAttrib(...);

window.resetGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

glPopAttrib(...);

// OpenGL code here...

Resize the render-texture.

The last parameter, settings, is useful if you want to enable multi-sampling or use the render-texture for OpenGL rendering that requires a depth or stencil buffer. Otherwise it is unnecessary, and you should leave this parameter at its default value.

After resizing, the contents of the render-texture are undefined. Call [RenderTexture::clear](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#aee353fc2cd35edf0747e710301af3e4c "Clear the entire target with a single color.") first to ensure a single color fill.

    | settings | Additional settings for the underlying OpenGL texture and context |

Returns
:   true if resizing has been successful, false if it failed

Activate or deactivate the render-texture for rendering.

This function makes the render-texture's context current for future OpenGL rendering operations (so you shouldn't care about it if you're not doing direct OpenGL stuff). Only one context can be current in a thread, so if you want to draw OpenGL geometry to another render target (like a [RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.")) don't forget to activate it again.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | active | true to activate, false to deactivate |

Returns
:   true if operation was successful, false otherwise

Change the current active view.

The view is like a 2D camera, it controls which part of the 2D scene is visible, and how it is viewed in the render target. The new view will affect everything that is drawn, until another view is set. The render target keeps its own copy of the view object, so it is not necessary to keep the original one alive after calling this function. To restore the original view of the target, you can pass the result of [getDefaultView()](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a7741129e3ef7ab4f0a40024fca13480c "Get the default view of the render target.") to this function.

:   |  |  |

## Detailed Description

[Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering.") that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.

[sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.") is the main class of the Graphics module.

It defines an OS window that can be painted using the other classes of the graphics module.

[sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.") is derived from [sf::Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering."), thus it inherits all its features: events, window management, OpenGL rendering, etc. See the documentation of [sf::Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering.") for a more complete description of all these features, as well as code examples.

On top of that, [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.") adds more features related to 2D drawing with the graphics module (see its base class [sf::RenderTarget](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html "Base class for all render targets (window, texture, ...)") for more details). Here is a typical rendering and event loop with a [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing."):

// Declare and create a new render-window

[sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html) window([sf::VideoMode](classsf_1_1VideoMode.html)({800, 600}), "SFML window");

// Limit the framerate to 60 frames per second (this step is optional)

window.[setFramerateLimit](classsf_1_1Window.html#af4322d315baf93405bf0d5087ad5e784)(60);

// The main loop - ends as soon as the window is closed

while (window.[isOpen](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#aa43559822564ef958dc664a90c57cba0)())

{

// Event processing

while (const std::optional event = window.[pollEvent](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a6090926b477e9d0a83854b94b9e1fd35)())

{

// Request for closing the window

if (event->is<[sf::Event::Closed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1Closed.html)>())

window.[close](classsf_1_1Window.html#ab1d808a3682db8d113d67354bcbd717d)();

}

// Clear the whole window before rendering a new frame

window.[clear](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#aee353fc2cd35edf0747e710301af3e4c)();

// Draw some graphical entities

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(sprite);

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(circle);

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(text);

// End the current frame and display its contents on screen

window.[display](classsf_1_1Window.html#adabf839cb103ac96cfc82f781638772a)();

}

Like [sf::Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering."), [sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html "Window that can serve as a target for 2D drawing.") is still able to render direct OpenGL stuff. It is even possible to mix together OpenGL calls and regular SFML drawing commands.

// Create the render window

[sf::RenderWindow](classsf_1_1RenderWindow.html) window([sf::VideoMode](classsf_1_1VideoMode.html)({800, 600}), "SFML OpenGL");

// Create a sprite and a text to display

const [sf::Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html) texture("circle.png");

[sf::Sprite](classsf_1_1Sprite.html) sprite(texture);

const [sf::Font](classsf_1_1Font.html) font("arial.ttf");

[sf::Text](classsf_1_1Text.html) text(font);

...

// Perform OpenGL initializations

glMatrixMode(GL\_PROJECTION);

...

// Start the rendering loop

while (window.[isOpen](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#aa43559822564ef958dc664a90c57cba0)())

{

// Process events

...

// Draw a background sprite

window.[pushGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a8d1998464ccc54e789aaf990242b47f7)();

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(sprite);

window.[popGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ad5a98401113df931ddcd54c080f7aa8e)();

// Draw a 3D object using OpenGL

glBegin(GL\_TRIANGLES);

glVertex3f(...);

...

glEnd();

// Draw text on top of the 3D object

window.[pushGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a8d1998464ccc54e789aaf990242b47f7)();

window.[draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39)(text);

window.[popGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ad5a98401113df931ddcd54c080f7aa8e)();

// Finally, display the rendered frame on screen

window.[display](classsf_1_1Window.html#adabf839cb103ac96cfc82f781638772a)();

}

|  |  | const [ContextSettings](structsf_1_1ContextSettings.html) & | *settings* = {} ) |

Construct a new window.

This constructor creates the window with the size and pixel depth defined in mode. An optional style can be passed to customize the look and behavior of the window (borders, title bar, resizable, closable, ...).

The last parameter is an optional structure specifying advanced OpenGL context settings such as anti-aliasing, depth-buffer bits, etc. You shouldn't care about these parameters for a regular usage of the graphics module.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | mode | Video mode to use (defines the width, height and depth of the rendering area of the window) |
    | title | Title of the window |
    | style | Window style, a bitwise OR combination of [sf::Style](namespacesf_1_1Style.html) enumerators |
    | state | Window state |
    | settings | Additional settings for the underlying OpenGL context |

## [◆](#ab1d808a3682db8d113d67354bcbd717d)close()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Window::close | ( |  | ) |  | | overridevirtualinherited |

Close the window and destroy all the attached resources.

After calling this function, the [sf::Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering.") instance remains valid and you can call [create()](classsf_1_1Window.html#ae77f112046c240b477963326e2363e18 "Create (or recreate) the window.") to recreate the window. All other functions such as [pollEvent()](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a6090926b477e9d0a83854b94b9e1fd35 "Pop the next event from the front of the FIFO event queue, if any, and return it.") or [display()](classsf_1_1Window.html#adabf839cb103ac96cfc82f781638772a "Display on screen what has been rendered to the window so far.") will still work (i.e. you don't have to test [isOpen()](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#aa43559822564ef958dc664a90c57cba0 "Tell whether or not the window is open.") every time), and will have no effect on closed windows.

Reimplemented from [sf::WindowBase](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a9a5ea0ba0ab584dbd11bbfea233b457f).

## [◆](#a0f3289445ce7103e85c56571c4bc0de9)handleEvents()

template<typename... Handlers>

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::WindowBase::handleEvents | ( | Handlers &&... | *handlers* | ) |  | | inherited |

Handle all pending events.

This function is not blocking: if there's no pending event then it will return without calling any of the handlers.

This function can take a variadic list of event handlers that each take a concrete event type as a single parameter. The event handlers can be any kind of callable object that has an operator() defined for a specific event type. Additionally a generic callable can also be provided that will be invoked for every event type. If both types of callables are provided, the callables taking concrete event types will be preferred over the generic callable by overload resolution. Generic callables can be used to customize handler dispatching based on the deduced type of the event and other information available at compile time.

Examples of callables:

* Lambda expressions: [&](const [sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html "Key pressed event subtype.")) { ... }
* Free functions: void handler(const [sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html "Key pressed event subtype.")&) { ... }

// Only provide handlers for concrete event types

window.handleEvents(

[&](const [sf::Event::Closed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1Closed.html)&) { /\* handle event \*/ },

[&](const [sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html)& keyPress) { /\* handle event \*/ }

);

[sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html)

Key pressed event subtype.

**Definition** [Event.hpp:97](Event_8hpp_source.html#l00096)

window.handleEvents(

[&](const auto& event)

{

if constexpr (std::is\_same\_v<std::decay\_t<decltype(event)>, [sf::Event::Closed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1Closed.html)>)

{

// Handle Closed

handleClosed();

}

else if constexpr (std::is\_same\_v<std::decay\_t<decltype(event)>, [sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html)>)

{

// Handle KeyPressed

handleKeyPressed(event);

}

else

{

// Handle non-KeyPressed

handleOtherEvents(event);

}

}

);

// Provide handlers for concrete types and fall back to generic handler

window.handleEvents(

[&](const [sf::Event::Closed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1Closed.html)&) { /\* handle event \*/ },

[&](const [sf::Event::KeyPressed](structsf_1_1Event_1_1KeyPressed.html)& keyPress) { /\* handle event \*/ },

[&](const auto& event) { /\* handle all other events \*/ }

);

Calling member functions is supported through lambda expressions.

[this](const auto& event) { handle(event); }

## [◆](#a07a8da6e2a9e3ce5f36344e3d8e7c41a)mapCoordsToPixel() [2/2]

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [Vector2i](namespacesf.html#af0ffe1b157a56931ee3a9a1a771a827a) sf::RenderTarget::mapCoordsToPixel | ( | [Vector2f](namespacesf.html#af14b40e82368dd601a7ef8037214804d) | *point*, | |  |  | const [View](classsf_1_1View.html) & | *view* ) const | | nodiscardinherited |

Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates.

This function finds the pixel of the render target that matches the given 2D point. In other words, it goes through the same process as the graphics card, to compute the final position of a rendered point.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (150, 75) in your 2D world may map to the pixel (10, 50) of your render target – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Point to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in target coordinates (pixels)

See also
:   [mapPixelToCoords](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a5ce02e4fd30e065c4dbeec239ae579b3 "Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates, using the current view.")

Convert a point from target coordinates to world coordinates.

This function finds the 2D position that matches the given pixel of the render target. In other words, it does the inverse of what the graphics card does, to find the initial position of a rendered pixel.

Initially, both coordinate systems (world units and target pixels) match perfectly. But if you define a custom view or resize your render target, this assertion is not true anymore, i.e. a point located at (10, 50) in your render target may map to the point (150, 75) in your 2D world – if the view is translated by (140, 25).

For render-windows, this function is typically used to find which point (or object) is located below the mouse cursor.

This version uses a custom view for calculations, see the other overload of the function if you want to use the current view of the render target.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | point | Pixel to convert |
    | view | The view to use for converting the point |

Returns
:   The converted point, in "world" units

See also
:   [mapCoordsToPixel](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ab473e0723ba16cf913deb03774c8458c "Convert a point from world coordinates to target coordinates, using the current view.")

## [◆](#a6090926b477e9d0a83854b94b9e1fd35)pollEvent()

| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | std::optional< [Event](classsf_1_1Event.html) > sf::WindowBase::pollEvent | ( |  | ) |  | | nodiscardinherited |

Pop the next event from the front of the FIFO event queue, if any, and return it.

This function is not blocking: if there's no pending event then it will return a std::nullopt. Note that more than one event may be present in the event queue, thus you should always call this function in a loop to make sure that you process every pending event.

while (const std::optional event = window.pollEvent())

{

// process event...

}

Returns
:   The event, otherwise std::nullopt if no events are pending

See also
:   [waitEvent](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#ab5975f6f6a06ecd6c18fa0f62cd1edf7 "Wait for an event and return it."), [handleEvents](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a0f3289445ce7103e85c56571c4bc0de9 "Handle all pending events.")

## [◆](#a8d1998464ccc54e789aaf990242b47f7)pushGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::RenderTarget::pushGLStates | ( |  | ) |  | | inherited |

Save the current OpenGL render states and matrices.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering. Combined with popGLStates, it ensures that:

* SFML's internal states are not messed up by your OpenGL code
* your OpenGL states are not modified by a call to a SFML function

More specifically, it must be used around code that calls draw functions. Example:

// OpenGL code here...

window.pushGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

window.popGLStates();

// OpenGL code here...

Note that this function is quite expensive: it saves all the possible OpenGL states and matrices, even the ones you don't care about. Therefore it should be used wisely. It is provided for convenience, but the best results will be achieved if you handle OpenGL states yourself (because you know which states have really changed, and need to be saved and restored). Take a look at the resetGLStates function if you do so.

See also
:   [popGLStates](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#ad5a98401113df931ddcd54c080f7aa8e "Restore the previously saved OpenGL render states and matrices.")

## [◆](#a448770d2372d8df0a1ad6b1c7cce3c89)requestFocus()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::WindowBase::requestFocus | ( |  | ) |  | | inherited |

Request the current window to be made the active foreground window.

At any given time, only one window may have the input focus to receive input events such as keystrokes or mouse events. If a window requests focus, it only hints to the operating system, that it would like to be focused. The operating system is free to deny the request. This is not to be confused with [setActive()](#a3f5476821139d5a7f0e4df19dab69b56 "Activate or deactivate the window as the current target for OpenGL rendering.").

See also
:   [hasFocus](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#ad87bd19e979c426cb819ccde8c95232e "Check whether the window has the input focus.")

## [◆](#aac7504990d27dada4bfe3c7866920765)resetGLStates()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::RenderTarget::resetGLStates | ( |  | ) |  | | inherited |

Reset the internal OpenGL states so that the target is ready for drawing.

This function can be used when you mix SFML drawing and direct OpenGL rendering, if you choose not to use pushGLStates/popGLStates. It makes sure that all OpenGL states needed by SFML are set, so that subsequent [draw()](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39 "Draw a drawable object to the render target.") calls will work as expected.

Example:

// OpenGL code here...

glPushAttrib(...);

window.resetGLStates();

window.draw(...);

window.draw(...);

glPopAttrib(...);

// OpenGL code here...

Activate or deactivate the window as the current target for OpenGL rendering.

A window is active only on the current thread, if you want to make it active on another thread you have to deactivate it on the previous thread first if it was active. Only one window can be active on a thread at a time, thus the window previously active (if any) automatically gets deactivated. This is not to be confused with [requestFocus()](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a448770d2372d8df0a1ad6b1c7cce3c89 "Request the current window to be made the active foreground window.").

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | active | true to activate, false to deactivate |

Returns
:   true if operation was successful, false otherwise

Reimplemented from [sf::RenderTarget](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#adc225ead22a70843ffa9b7eebefa0ce1).

## [◆](#af4322d315baf93405bf0d5087ad5e784)setFramerateLimit()

| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Window::setFramerateLimit | ( | unsigned int | *limit* | ) |  | | inherited |

Limit the framerate to a maximum fixed frequency.

If a limit is set, the window will use a small delay after each call to [display()](classsf_1_1Window.html#adabf839cb103ac96cfc82f781638772a "Display on screen what has been rendered to the window so far.") to ensure that the current frame lasted long enough to match the framerate limit. SFML will try to match the given limit as much as it can, but since it internally uses [sf::sleep](group__system.html#gab8c0d1f966b4e5110fd370b662d8c11b "Make the current thread sleep for a given duration."), whose precision depends on the underlying OS, the results may be a little imprecise as well (for example, you can get 65 FPS when requesting 60).

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | limit | Framerate limit, in frames per seconds (use 0 to disable limit) |

## [◆](#a59041c4556e0351048f8aff366034f61)setVerticalSyncEnabled()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Window::setVerticalSyncEnabled | ( | bool | *enabled* | ) |  | | inherited |

Enable or disable vertical synchronization.

Activating vertical synchronization will limit the number of frames displayed to the refresh rate of the monitor. This can avoid some visual artifacts, and limit the framerate to a good value (but not constant across different computers).

Vertical synchronization is disabled by default.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | enabled | true to enable v-sync, false to deactivate it |

## [◆](#a063db6dd0a14913504af30e50cb6d946)setView()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::RenderTarget::setView | ( | const [View](classsf_1_1View.html) & | *view* | ) |  | | inherited |

Change the current active view.

The view is like a 2D camera, it controls which part of the 2D scene is visible, and how it is viewed in the render target. The new view will affect everything that is drawn, until another view is set. The render target keeps its own copy of the view object, so it is not necessary to keep the original one alive after calling this function. To restore the original view of the target, you can pass the result of [getDefaultView()](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a7741129e3ef7ab4f0a40024fca13480c "Get the default view of the render target.") to this function.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | view | New view to use |

See also
:   [getView](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#adbf8dc5a1f4abbe15a3fbb915844c7ea "Get the view currently in use in the render target."), [getDefaultView](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a7741129e3ef7ab4f0a40024fca13480c "Get the default view of the render target.")

## [◆](#ab5975f6f6a06ecd6c18fa0f62cd1edf7)waitEvent()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | std::optional< [Event](classsf_1_1Event.html) > sf::WindowBase::waitEvent | ( | [Time](classsf_1_1Time.html) | *timeout* = [Time::Zero](classsf_1_1Time.html#a8db127b632fa8da21550e7282af11fa0) | ) |  | | nodiscardinherited |

Wait for an event and return it.

This function is blocking: if there's no pending event then it will wait until an event is received or until the provided timeout elapses. Only if an error or a timeout occurs the returned event will be std::nullopt. This function is typically used when you have a thread that is dedicated to events handling: you want to make this thread sleep as long as no new event is received.

while (const std::optional event = window.waitEvent())

{

// process event...

}

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | timeout | Maximum time to wait ([Time::Zero](classsf_1_1Time.html#a8db127b632fa8da21550e7282af11fa0 "Predefined \"zero\" time value.") for infinite) |

Returns
:   The event, otherwise std::nullopt on timeout or if window was closed

See also
:   [pollEvent](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a6090926b477e9d0a83854b94b9e1fd35 "Pop the next event from the front of the FIFO event queue, if any, and return it."), [handleEvents](classsf_1_1WindowBase.html#a0f3289445ce7103e85c56571c4bc0de9 "Handle all pending events.")

## Detailed Description

[Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") class (vertex, geometry and fragment)

Shaders are programs written using a specific language, executed directly by the graphics card and allowing to apply real-time operations to the rendered entities.

There are three kinds of shaders:

* Vertex shaders, that process vertices
* Geometry shaders, that process primitives
* Fragment (pixel) shaders, that process pixels

A [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") can be composed of either a vertex shader alone, a geometry shader alone, a fragment shader alone, or any combination of them. (see the variants of the load functions).

Shaders are written in GLSL, which is a C-like language dedicated to OpenGL shaders. You'll probably need to learn its basics before writing your own shaders for SFML.

Like any C/C++ program, a GLSL shader has its own variables called *uniforms* that you can set from your C++ application. [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") handles different types of uniforms:

* scalars: `float`, `int`, `bool`
* vectors (2, 3 or 4 components)
* matrices (3x3 or 4x4)
* samplers (textures)

Some SFML-specific types can be converted:

* [sf::Color](classsf_1_1Color.html "Utility class for manipulating RGBA colors.") as a 4D vector (`vec4`)
* [sf::Transform](classsf_1_1Transform.html "3x3 transform matrix") as matrices (`mat3` or `mat4`)

Every uniform variable in a shader can be set through one of the [setUniform()](#abf78e3bea1e9b0bab850b6b0a0de29c7 "Specify value for float uniform.") or [setUniformArray()](#a731d3b9953c50fe7d3fb03340b97deff "Specify values for float[] array uniform.") overloads. For example, if you have a shader with the following uniforms:

uniform float offset;

uniform vec3 point;

uniform vec4 color;

uniform mat4 matrix;

uniform sampler2D overlay;

uniform sampler2D current;

You can set their values from C++ code as follows, using the types defined in the [sf::Glsl](namespacesf_1_1Glsl.html "Namespace with GLSL types.") namespace:

shader.setUniform("offset", 2.f);

shader.setUniform("point", [sf::Vector3f](namespacesf.html#aabc495912efba35400b484ea842664d0)(0.5f, 0.8f, 0.3f));

shader.setUniform("color", [sf::Glsl::Vec4](namespacesf_1_1Glsl.html#abf169ad4f8b5405d6b2f37ecd9d28cbd)(color)); // color is a sf::Color

shader.setUniform("matrix", [sf::Glsl::Mat4](namespacesf_1_1Glsl.html#ac7e4d95124aac05edea445249a71c00c)(transform)); // transform is a sf::Transform

shader.setUniform("overlay", texture); // texture is a sf::Texture

shader.setUniform("current", [sf::Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d));

The special [Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d "Represents the texture of the object being drawn.") argument maps the given `sampler2D` uniform to the current texture of the object being drawn (which cannot be known in advance).

To apply a shader to a drawable, you must pass it as an additional parameter to the [RenderWindow::draw](classsf_1_1RenderTarget.html#a12417a3bcc245c41d957b29583556f39 "Draw a drawable object to the render target.") function:

window.draw(sprite, &shader);

... which is in fact just a shortcut for this:

[sf::RenderStates](structsf_1_1RenderStates.html) states;

states.[shader](structsf_1_1RenderStates.html#ad4f79ecdd0c60ed0d24fbe555b221bd8) = &shader;

window.draw(sprite, states);

[sf::RenderStates](structsf_1_1RenderStates.html)

[sf::RenderStates::shader](structsf_1_1RenderStates.html#ad4f79ecdd0c60ed0d24fbe555b221bd8)

const Shader \* shader

Shader.

**Definition** [RenderStates.hpp:136](RenderStates_8hpp_source.html#l00136)

In the code above we pass a pointer to the shader, because it may be null (which means "no shader").

Shaders can be used on any drawable, but some combinations are not interesting. For example, using a vertex shader on a [sf::Sprite](classsf_1_1Sprite.html "Drawable representation of a texture, with its own transformations, color, etc.") is limited because there are only 4 vertices, the sprite would have to be subdivided in order to apply wave effects. Another bad example is a fragment shader with [sf::Text](classsf_1_1Text.html "Graphical text that can be drawn to a render target."): the texture of the text is not the actual text that you see on screen, it is a big texture containing all the characters of the font in an arbitrary order; thus, texture lookups on pixels other than the current one may not give you the expected result.

Shaders can also be used to apply global post-effects to the current contents of the target. This can be done in two different ways:

* draw everything to a [sf::RenderTexture](classsf_1_1RenderTexture.html "Target for off-screen 2D rendering into a texture."), then draw it to the main target using the shader
* draw everything directly to the main target, then use [sf::Texture::update](classsf_1_1Texture.html#aeaf40495f5860120b95d190def4f8bbc "Update the whole texture from an array of pixels.")([Window](classsf_1_1Window.html "Window that serves as a target for OpenGL rendering.")&) to copy its contents to a texture and draw it to the main target using the shader

The first technique is more optimized because it doesn't involve retrieving the target's pixels to system memory, but the second one doesn't impact the rendering process and can be easily inserted anywhere without impacting all the code.

Like [sf::Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html "Image living on the graphics card that can be used for drawing.") that can be used as a raw OpenGL texture, [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") can also be used directly as a raw shader for custom OpenGL geometry.

Construct from a shader file.

This constructor loads a single shader, vertex, geometry or fragment, identified by the second argument. The source must be a text file containing a valid shader in GLSL language. GLSL is a C-like language dedicated to OpenGL shaders; you'll probably need to read a good documentation for it before writing your own shaders.

Construct from vertex and fragment shader files.

This constructor loads both the vertex and the fragment shaders. If one of them fails to load, the shader is left empty (the valid shader is unloaded). The sources must be text files containing valid shaders in GLSL language. GLSL is a C-like language dedicated to OpenGL shaders; you'll probably need to read a good documentation for it before writing your own shaders.

## [◆](#a09778f78afcbeb854d608c8dacd8ea30)bind()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Shader::bind | ( | const [Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html) \* | *shader* | ) |  | | static |

Bind a shader for rendering.

This function is not part of the graphics API, it mustn't be used when drawing SFML entities. It must be used only if you mix [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") with OpenGL code.

[sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html) s1, s2;

...

sf::Shader::bind(&s1);

// draw OpenGL stuff that use s1...

[sf::Shader::bind](#a09778f78afcbeb854d608c8dacd8ea30)(&s2);

// draw OpenGL stuff that use s2...

[sf::Shader::bind](#a09778f78afcbeb854d608c8dacd8ea30)(nullptr);

// draw OpenGL stuff that use no shader...

[sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html)

Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)

Parameters

## [◆](#ad22474690bafe4a305c1b9826b1bd86a)isAvailable()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |

| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | bool sf::Shader::isAvailable | ( |  | ) |  | | staticnodiscard |

Tell whether or not the system supports shaders.

This function should always be called before using the shader features. If it returns false, then any attempt to use [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") will fail.

Returns
:   true if shaders are supported, false otherwise

## [◆](#a45db14baf1bbc688577f81813b1fce96)isGeometryAvailable()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | bool sf::Shader::isGeometryAvailable | ( |  | ) |  | | staticnodiscard |

Tell whether or not the system supports geometry shaders.

This function should always be called before using the geometry shader features. If it returns false, then any attempt to use [sf::Shader](classsf_1_1Shader.html "Shader class (vertex, geometry and fragment)") geometry shader features will fail.

This function can only return true if [isAvailable()](#ad22474690bafe4a305c1b9826b1bd86a "Tell whether or not the system supports shaders.") would also return true, since shaders in general have to be supported in order for geometry shaders to be supported as well.

Note: The first call to this function, whether by your code or SFML will result in a context switch.

Returns
:   true if geometry shaders are supported, false otherwise

If color conversions are used, the ivec4 uniform in GLSL will hold the same values as the original [sf::Color](classsf_1_1Color.html "Utility class for manipulating RGBA colors.") instance. For example, [sf::Color(255, 127, 0, 255)](classsf_1_1Color.html "Utility class for manipulating RGBA colors.") is mapped to ivec4(255, 127, 0, 255).

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | name | Name of the uniform variable in GLSL |
    | vector | Value of the ivec4 vector |

Specify value for `vec4` uniform.

This overload can also be called with [sf::Color](classsf_1_1Color.html "Utility class for manipulating RGBA colors.") objects that are converted to [sf::Glsl::Vec4](namespacesf_1_1Glsl.html#abf169ad4f8b5405d6b2f37ecd9d28cbd "4D float vector (vec4 in GLSL)").

It is important to note that the components of the color are normalized before being passed to the shader. Therefore, they are converted from range [0 .. 255] to range [0 .. 1]. For example, a [sf::Color(255, 127, 0, 255)](classsf_1_1Color.html "Utility class for manipulating RGBA colors.") will be transformed to a vec4(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) in the shader.

|  |  | const [Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html) & | *texture* ) |

Specify a texture as `sampler2D` uniform.

*name* is the name of the variable to change in the shader. The corresponding parameter in the shader must be a 2D texture (`sampler2D` GLSL type).

Example:

uniform sampler2D the\_texture; // this is the variable in the shader

[sf::Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html) texture;

...

shader.setUniform("the\_texture", texture);

[sf::Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html)

Image living on the graphics card that can be used for drawing.

**Definition** [Texture.hpp:56](Texture_8hpp_source.html#l00055)

It is important to note that texture must remain alive as long as the shader uses it, no copy is made internally.

To use the texture of the object being drawn, which cannot be known in advance, you can pass the special value [sf::Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d "Represents the texture of the object being drawn."):

shader.setUniform("the\_texture", [sf::Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d)).

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | name | Name of the texture in the shader |
    | texture | [Texture](classsf_1_1Texture.html "Image living on the graphics card that can be used for drawing.") to assign |

## [◆](#ab18f531e1f726b88fec1cf5a1e6af26d)setUniform() [12/17]

| void sf::Shader::setUniform | ( | const std::string & | *name*, |

Specify current texture as `sampler2D` uniform.

This overload maps a shader texture variable to the texture of the object being drawn, which cannot be known in advance. The second argument must be [sf::Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d "Represents the texture of the object being drawn."). The corresponding parameter in the shader must be a 2D texture (`sampler2D` GLSL type).

Example:

uniform sampler2D current; // this is the variable in the shader

shader.setUniform("current", [sf::Shader::CurrentTexture](#ac84c7953eec2e19358ea6e2cc5385b8d));

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | name | Name of the texture in the shader |

## Detailed Description

Base class for textured shapes with outline.

[sf::Shape](classsf_1_1Shape.html "Base class for textured shapes with outline.") is a drawable class that allows to define and display a custom convex shape on a render target.

It's only an abstract base, it needs to be specialized for concrete types of shapes (circle, rectangle, convex polygon, star, ...).

In addition to the attributes provided by the specialized shape classes, a shape always has the following attributes:

* a texture
* a texture rectangle
* a fill color
* an outline color
* an outline thickness

Each feature is optional, and can be disabled easily:

* the texture can be null
* the fill/outline colors can be [sf::Color::Transparent](classsf_1_1Color.html#a569b45471737f770656f50ae7bbac292 "Transparent (black) predefined color.")
* the outline thickness can be zero

You can write your own derived shape class, there are only two virtual functions to override:

* getPointCount must return the number of points of the shape
* getPoint must return the points of the shape

See also
:   [sf::RectangleShape](classsf_1_1RectangleShape.html "Specialized shape representing a rectangle."), [sf::CircleShape](classsf_1_1CircleShape.html "Specialized shape representing a circle."), [sf::ConvexShape](classsf_1_1ConvexShape.html "Specialized shape representing a convex polygon."), [sf::Transformable](classsf_1_1Transformable.html "Decomposed transform defined by a position, a rotation and a scale.")

Definition at line [54](Shape_8hpp_source.html#l00054) of file [Shape.hpp](Shape_8hpp_source.html).

## [◆](#ac0e29425d908d5442060cc44790fe4da)getGlobalBounds()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | [FloatRect](namespacesf.html#a701020eb396e62ba560619e68c689a38) sf::Shape::getGlobalBounds | ( |  | ) | const | | nodiscard |

Get the global (non-minimal) bounding rectangle of the entity.

The returned rectangle is in global coordinates, which means that it takes into account the transformations (translation, rotation, scale, ...) that are applied to the entity. In other words, this function returns the bounds of the shape in the global 2D world's coordinate system.

This function does not necessarily return the *minimal* bounding rectangle. It merely ensures that the returned rectangle covers all the vertices (but possibly more). This allows for a fast approximation of the bounds as a first check; you may want to use more precise checks on top of that.

Returns
:   Global bounding rectangle of the entity

Set the fill color of the shape.

This color is modulated (multiplied) with the shape's texture if any. It can be used to colorize the shape, or change its global opacity. You can use [sf::Color::Transparent](classsf_1_1Color.html#a569b45471737f770656f50ae7bbac292 "Transparent (black) predefined color.") to make the inside of the shape transparent, and have the outline alone. By default, the shape's fill color is opaque white.

The origin of an object defines the center point for all transformations (position, scale, rotation). The coordinates of this point must be relative to the top-left corner of the object, and ignore all transformations (position, scale, rotation). The default origin of a transformable object is (0, 0).

Change the source texture of the shape.

The texture argument refers to a texture that must exist as long as the shape uses it. Indeed, the shape doesn't store its own copy of the texture, but rather keeps a pointer to the one that you passed to this function. If the source texture is destroyed and the shape tries to use it, the behavior is undefined. texture can be a null pointer to disable texturing. If resetRect is true, the TextureRect property of the shape is automatically adjusted to the size of the new texture. If it is false, the texture rect is left unchanged.

## Detailed Description

Base class for all the socket types.

This class mainly defines internal stuff to be used by derived classes.

The only public features that it defines, and which is therefore common to all the socket classes, is the blocking state. All sockets can be set as blocking or non-blocking.

In blocking mode, socket functions will hang until the operation completes, which means that the entire program (well, in fact the current thread if you use multiple ones) will be stuck waiting for your socket operation to complete.

In non-blocking mode, all the socket functions will return immediately. If the socket is not ready to complete the requested operation, the function simply returns the proper status code ([Socket::Status::NotReady](#a51bf0fd51057b98a10fbb866246176dcadd353567e8118a2b8df4e822e59084ab "The socket is not ready to send / receive data yet.")).

The default mode, which is blocking, is the one that is generally used, in combination with threads or selectors. The non-blocking mode is rather used in real-time applications that run an endless loop that can poll the socket often enough, and cannot afford blocking this loop.

See also
:   [sf::TcpListener](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html "Socket that listens to new TCP connections."), [sf::TcpSocket](classsf_1_1TcpSocket.html "Specialized socket using the TCP protocol."), [sf::UdpSocket](classsf_1_1UdpSocket.html "Specialized socket using the UDP protocol.")

## [◆](#a165fc1423e281ea2714c70303d3a9782)setBlocking()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| void sf::Socket::setBlocking | ( | bool | *blocking* | ) |  |

Set the blocking state of the socket.

In blocking mode, calls will not return until they have completed their task. For example, a call to Receive in blocking mode won't return until some data was actually received. In non-blocking mode, calls will always return immediately, using the return code to signal whether there was data available or not. By default, all sockets are blocking.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | blocking | true to set the socket as blocking, false for non-blocking |

See also
:   [isBlocking](#ab1ceca9ac114b8baeeda3b34a0aca468 "Tell whether the socket is in blocking or non-blocking mode.")

## Detailed Description

Multiplexer that allows to read from multiple sockets.

[Socket](classsf_1_1Socket.html "Base class for all the socket types.") selectors provide a way to wait until some data is available on a set of sockets, instead of just one.

This is convenient when you have multiple sockets that may possibly receive data, but you don't know which one will be ready first. In particular, it avoids to use a thread for each socket; with selectors, a single thread can handle all the sockets.

All types of sockets can be used in a selector:

* [sf::TcpListener](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html "Socket that listens to new TCP connections.")
* [sf::TcpSocket](classsf_1_1TcpSocket.html "Specialized socket using the TCP protocol.")
* [sf::UdpSocket](classsf_1_1UdpSocket.html "Specialized socket using the UDP protocol.")

A selector doesn't store its own copies of the sockets (socket classes are not copyable anyway), it simply keeps a reference to the original sockets that you pass to the "add" function. Therefore, you can't use the selector as a socket container, you must store them outside and make sure that they are alive as long as they are used in the selector.

Using a selector is simple:

* populate the selector with all the sockets that you want to observe
* make it wait until there is data available on any of the sockets
* test each socket to find out which ones are ready

Usage example:

// Create a socket to listen to new connections

[sf::TcpListener](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html) listener;

if (listener.[listen](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html#a4e1610356eb74ff5c699b673e550ea82)(55001) != [sf::Socket::Status::Done](classsf_1_1Socket.html#a51bf0fd51057b98a10fbb866246176dcaf92965e2c8a7afb3c1b9a5c09a263636))

{

// Handle error...

}

// Create a list to store the future clients

std::vector<sf::TcpSocket> clients;

// Create a selector

[sf::SocketSelector](classsf_1_1SocketSelector.html) selector;

// Add the listener to the selector

selector.[add](#ade952013232802ff7b9b33668f8d2096)(listener);

// Endless loop that waits for new connections

while (running)

{

// Make the selector wait for data on any socket

if (selector.[wait](#a9cfda5475f17925e65889394d70af702)())

{

// Test the listener

if (selector.[isReady](#a917a4bac708290a6782e6686fd3bf889)(listener))

{

// The listener is ready: there is a pending connection

[sf::TcpSocket](classsf_1_1TcpSocket.html) client;

if (listener.[accept](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html#ae2c83ce5a64d50b68180c46bef0a7346)(client) == [sf::Socket::Status::Done](classsf_1_1Socket.html#a51bf0fd51057b98a10fbb866246176dcaf92965e2c8a7afb3c1b9a5c09a263636))

{

// Add the new client to the selector so that we will

// be notified when they send something

selector.[add](#ade952013232802ff7b9b33668f8d2096)(client);

// Add the new client to the clients list

clients.push\_back(std::move(client));

}

else

{

// Handle error...

}

}

else

{

// The listener socket is not ready, test all other sockets (the clients)

for (sf::TcpSocket& client : clients)

{

if (selector.[isReady](#a917a4bac708290a6782e6686fd3bf889)(client))

{

// The client has sent some data, we can receive it

sf::Packet packet;

if (client.[receive](classsf_1_1TcpSocket.html#a90ce50811ea61d4f00efc62bb99ae1af)(packet) == [sf::Socket::Status::Done](classsf_1_1Socket.html#a51bf0fd51057b98a10fbb866246176dcaf92965e2c8a7afb3c1b9a5c09a263636))

{

...

}

}

}

}

}

| void sf::SocketSelector::add | ( | [Socket](classsf_1_1Socket.html) & | *socket* | ) |  |

Add a new socket to the selector.

This function keeps a weak reference to the socket, so you have to make sure that the socket is not destroyed while it is stored in the selector. This function does nothing if the socket is not valid.

Parameters

    | --- | --- |

## [◆](#a917a4bac708290a6782e6686fd3bf889)isReady()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | bool sf::SocketSelector::isReady | ( | [Socket](classsf_1_1Socket.html) & | *socket* | ) | const | | nodiscard |

Test a socket to know if it is ready to receive data.

This function must be used after a call to Wait, to know which sockets are ready to receive data. If a socket is ready, a call to receive will never block because we know that there is data available to read. Note that if this function returns true for a [TcpListener](classsf_1_1TcpListener.html "Socket that listens to new TCP connections."), this means that it is ready to accept a new connection.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | socket | [Socket](classsf_1_1Socket.html "Base class for all the socket types.") to test |

Returns
:   true if the socket is ready to read, false otherwise

See also
:   [isReady](#a917a4bac708290a6782e6686fd3bf889 "Test a socket to know if it is ready to receive data.")

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | bool sf::SocketSelector::wait | ( | [Time](classsf_1_1Time.html) | *timeout* = [Time::Zero](classsf_1_1Time.html#a8db127b632fa8da21550e7282af11fa0) | ) |  | | nodiscard |

Wait until one or more sockets are ready to receive.

This function returns as soon as at least one socket has some data available to be received. To know which sockets are ready, use the isReady function. If you use a timeout and no socket is ready before the timeout is over, the function returns false.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | timeout | Maximum time to wait, (use [Time::Zero](classsf_1_1Time.html#a8db127b632fa8da21550e7282af11fa0 "Predefined \"zero\" time value.") for infinity) |

Returns
:   true if there are sockets ready, false otherwise

## Detailed Description

Regular sound that can be played in the audio environment.

[sf::Sound](classsf_1_1Sound.html "Regular sound that can be played in the audio environment.") is the class to use to play sounds.

It provides:

* Control (play, pause, stop)
* Ability to modify output parameters in real-time (pitch, volume, ...)
* 3D spatial features (position, attenuation, ...).

[sf::Sound](classsf_1_1Sound.html "Regular sound that can be played in the audio environment.") is perfect for playing short sounds that can fit in memory and require no latency, like foot steps or gun shots. For longer sounds, like background musics or long speeches, rather see [sf::Music](classsf_1_1Music.html "Streamed music played from an audio file.") (which is based on streaming).

In order to work, a sound must be given a buffer of audio data to play. Audio data (samples) is stored in [sf::SoundBuffer](classsf_1_1SoundBuffer.html "Storage for audio samples defining a sound."), and attached to a sound when it is created or with the [setBuffer()](#a8b395e9713d0efa48a18628c8ec1972e "Set the source buffer containing the audio data to play.") function. The buffer object attached to a sound must remain alive as long as the sound uses it. Note that multiple sounds can use the same sound buffer at the same time.

Usage example:

const [sf::SoundBuffer](classsf_1_1SoundBuffer.html) buffer("sound.wav");

[sf::Sound](classsf_1_1Sound.html) sound(buffer);

sound.play();

## [◆](#ab13ce12bd2ef4856511824557b07cce5)EffectProcessor

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| |  | | --- | | using [sf::SoundSource::EffectProcessor](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html#ab13ce12bd2ef4856511824557b07cce5) | | inherited |

**Initial value:**

std::function<

void(const float\* inputFrames, unsigned int& inputFrameCount, float\* outputFrames, unsigned int& outputFrameCount, unsigned int frameChannelCount)>

Callable that is provided with sound data for processing.

When the audio engine sources sound data from sound sources it will pass the data through an effects processor if one is set. The sound data will already be converted to the internal floating point format.

[Sound](classsf_1_1Sound.html "Regular sound that can be played in the audio environment.") data that is processed this way is provided in frames. Each frame contains 1 floating point sample per channel. If e.g. the data source provides stereo data, each frame will contain 2 floats.

The effects processor function takes 4 parameters:

* The input data frames, channels interleaved
* The number of input data frames available
* The buffer to write output data frames to, channels interleaved
* The number of output data frames that the output buffer can hold
* The channel count

The input and output frame counts are in/out parameters.

When this function is called, the input count will contain the number of frames available in the input buffer. The output count will contain the size of the output buffer i.e. the maximum number of frames that can be written to the output buffer.

Attempting to read more frames than the input frame count or write more frames than the output frame count will result in undefined behaviour.

It is important to note that the channel count of the audio engine currently sourcing data from this sound will always be provided in frameChannelCount. This can be different from the channel count of the sound source so make sure to size necessary processing buffers according to the engine channel count and not the sound source channel count.

When done processing the frames, the input and output frame counts must be updated to reflect the actual number of frames that were read from the input and written to the output.

The processing function should always try to process as much sound data as possible i.e. always try to fill the output buffer to the maximum. In certain situations for specific effects it can be possible that the input frame count and output frame count aren't equal. As long as the frame counts are updated accordingly this is perfectly valid.

If the audio engine determines that no audio data is available from the data source, the input data frames pointer is set to nullptr and the input frame count is set to 0. In this case it is up to the function to decide how to handle the situation. For specific effects e.g. Echo/Delay buffered data might still be able to be written to the output buffer even if there is no longer any input data.

An important thing to remember is that this function is directly called by the audio engine. Because the audio engine runs on an internal thread of its own, make sure access to shared data is synchronized appropriately.

Because this function is stored by the [SoundSource](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html "Base class defining a sound's properties.") object it will be able to be called as long as the [SoundSource](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html "Base class defining a sound's properties.") object hasn't yet been destroyed. Make sure that any data this function references outlives the [SoundSource](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html "Base class defining a sound's properties.") object otherwise use-after-free errors will occur.

## [◆](#a969d9c9c5e742ba91a39f7f12fed9096)play()

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::Sound::play | ( |  | ) |  | | overridevirtual |

Start or resume playing the sound.

This function starts the stream if it was stopped, resumes it if it was paused, and restarts it from beginning if it was it already playing. This function uses its own thread so that it doesn't block the rest of the program while the sound is played.

See also
:   [pause](#a24b31c90af33c6bdc302f876abdf8a39 "Pause the sound."), [stop](#a90c9112782d5bc424a8e9e3ee7ecef19 "stop playing the sound")

## [◆](#aa2adff44cd2f8b4e3c7315d7c2a45626)setAttenuation()

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| |  |  |  |  |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | void sf::SoundSource::setAttenuation | ( | float | *attenuation* | ) |  | | inherited |

Set the attenuation factor of the sound.

The attenuation is a multiplicative factor which makes the sound more or less loud according to its distance from the listener. An attenuation of 0 will produce a non-attenuated sound, i.e. its volume will always be the same whether it is heard from near or from far. On the other hand, an attenuation value such as 100 will make the sound fade out very quickly as it gets further from the listener. The default value of the attenuation is 1.

Parameters
:   |  |  |
    | --- | --- |
    | attenuation | New attenuation factor of the sound |

See also
:   [getAttenuation](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html#a8ad7dafb4f1b4afbc638cebe24f48cc9 "Get the attenuation factor of the sound."), [setMinDistance](classsf_1_1SoundSource.html#a75bbc2c34addc8b25a14edb908508afe "Set the minimum distance of the sound.")
